analysis.one_liner: Closes loopholes that let US corporations avoid taxes by shifting profits and headquarters overseas.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was introduced in March 2021, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how the tax code treats money that US-based companies earn through foreign subsidiaries. It would tax profits shifted to low-tax countries in the year they are earned, deny deductions for interest used to load debt onto US operations, tighten rules so companies that relocate their headquarters abroad purely to cut their tax bill still owe US taxes, and treat foreign corporations actually run from the United States as domestic for tax purposes. It went to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would bear a smaller share of federal revenue if corporations could no longer dodge taxes by booking profits in low-tax countries, locating debt in the US, and reincorporating overseas.

how_it_helps.text: Requires US companies to include profits earned through foreign subsidiaries in their taxable income in the current year, ending rules that let some foreign profits go untaxed, and repeals the reduced tax rate on foreign income and on 'foreign-derived intangible income' [S2] [S3].
Applies the foreign tax credit limitation country by country, so companies cannot use low taxes paid in one country to shield high-tax income shifted elsewhere [S2] [S3].

Tightens the rules for inverted corporations — companies that acquire a foreign firm to reincorporate in a low-tax country — including by counting management and control located in the US, and treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the US as domestic for tax purposes [S2] [S3].

Limits deductions for interest expense by large multinational groups, discouraging the practice of loading debt onto US operations to shrink US taxable income, and taxes foreign base company oil-related income as it treats other offshore profits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that currently shift profits and debt overseas to cut their US tax bill, including companies that relocated their headquarters abroad for tax reasons; higher corporate tax bills could ultimately be passed to consumers or shareholders.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise effective taxes on US-headquartered multinationals, and opponents of such measures argue higher taxes on companies competing globally can reduce investment in the US or be passed to consumers; the bill text itself makes no provision for offsetting these costs [S3].

Some provisions, such as taxing corporations managed from the US with $50 million or more in assets and limits keyed to consolidated financial statements, would add significant complexity and compliance burden, and parts rely on Treasury regulations to define key terms [S3].
The bill attracted only 8 cosponsors, all Democrats, suggesting limited appetite even among senators to move it as a standalone measure [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions target widely recognized tax-avoidance structures — profit shifting, interest stripping, and headquarters relocation — and would broaden the tax base; the main honest costs are higher effective taxes on multinationals that may be partly passed to consumers, real compliance complexity in provisions like the country-by-country credit and management-and-control tests, and reliance on Treasury regulations to fill in key definitions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Whitehouse on March 11, 2021, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
That referral was the bill's last action of record; the Finance Committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended [S5].
Eight senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill; no Republican sponsor or cosponsor ever signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations that benefit from the current treatment of offshore profits, interest deductions, and inverted headquarters; they keep the existing rules because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: US Senator from Rhode Island (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought cosponsors; it was his measure to tax offshore-shifted profits and inverted corporations.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Dick Durbin, Chris Van Hollen, Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, Jeff Merkley, and Jack Reed.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred to the committee; it received no further action of record.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored or spoke for the bill during its life, leaving it without any path in a chamber where most legislation needs bipartisan agreement to advance.

sides.party_line_note: All nine named supporters were Democrats; no Republican ever cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where opposition could be recorded.

industries.note: The bill would tax profits they currently shift to low-tax foreign jurisdictions in the year earned, end favorable rates on foreign income, and limit interest deductions that shrink US taxable income. Their gain under current law is federal revenue ordinary taxpayers otherwise make up.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with foreign operations
industries.note: The bill taxes foreign base company oil-related income, ending favorable treatment for certain offshore oil and gas profits booked abroad.

The bill would treat foreign corporations with $50 million or more in assets under management that are run from the United States as domestic for tax purposes, sweeping many US-managed foreign investment vehicles into the US tax net.
